items.name: Botany -- CONTROL r0
items.response:
A sudden dieback confronts the investigator with two competing hypotheses, biotic invasion and abiotic water limitation, and discriminating between them rests on independent lines of evidence rather than on the appearance of the crowns alone. Attribution therefore begins on the organismal side of the problem. Plant pathologists isolate candidate organisms from the margins of necrotic lesions on symptomatic trees, and those isolations in turn give rise to inoculation trials on healthy saplings that test whether an isolate reproduces the field symptoms. Only afterwards does the decisive methodological requirement come into play: Koch's postulates require re-isolating the organism from inoculated trees that develop the same symptoms. Koch's postulates are satisfied without reproducing symptoms in a healthy host plant. The insistence on re-isolation from inoculated trees that have expressed the field syndrome cannot be squared with satisfaction of the postulates in the absence of any reproduced symptoms in a healthy host; the two formulations of the standard cannot both stand.

Mapping the mortality across the stand is the standard complement to the laboratory work, since the two hypotheses predict quite different geometries on the ground. Clustered mortality expanding along an advancing front is characteristic of an infectious agent, whereas mortality distributed according to soil water-holding capacity and slope position indicates drought stress. Drought-induced mortality always appears as a tight cluster spreading along a single advancing front. Yet mortality that tracks the water storage of the soil and position on the slope rules out drought's invariably taking the shape of one tight, advancing cluster; both patterns cannot be true of water-limited dieback at once.

Site history, reconstructed from meteorological records, tree rings and soil assays, narrows the field further. At least one of the following is the case, and perhaps both: the stand experienced a three-year precipitation deficit before the dieback, or an introduced pathogen was established in the soil of the affected stand. Where the historical record leaves the matter underdetermined, genomic analysis adjudicates. Whole-genome sequencing of isolates can show whether the outbreak population descends from one introduced lineage, and it is precisely that genomic reading which demonstrates that low genetic diversity among isolates points to a recent introduction rather than a long-resident population.

The establishment of an introduced pathogen in that stand's soil, for its part, sets a regulatory sequence in motion. Because the scarcity of genetic variation among the isolates marks the population as newly arrived in the region, quarantine and nursery movement restrictions follow confirmation of an introduced forest pathogen in a region.

The sequencing of the outbreak population returned the finding that ultimately settled the attribution. The outbreak isolates belonged to a single clonal lineage; that is, every sampled isolate was a genetically identical copy of one genotype. A population of that structure is the signature of an organism newly arrived and spreading from a single founding event, and it is this genomic result, anchored to the completed pathogenicity trials and to the mapped geometry of mortality, that an expert panel treats as decisive.
